subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: When Irawati joined our class in the middle of term, she stood by the door holding her bag with both hands. I remembered my own first day at a new school and how loud it felt. I smiled and waved, and she waved back very small. At lunch I patted the empty place next to me. “Do you want to sit here?” She nodded and sat. I offered her half of my orange, and she took one piece. I'm not chatty, so I just showed her where the water cooler and library are. She smiled all the way back to class. I'm Sarika, and that is enough for me.

qa.q: Where was Irawati standing when she first came in?
qa.a: By the door, holding her bag with both hands.

qa.q: What was Sarika feeling when smiling and waving at Irawati?
qa.a: Sarika felt sympathy for the newcomer, remembering how loud a first day at a new school felt, and wanted Irawati to feel welcome.

qa.q: What can a shy child do to welcome a new classmate?
qa.a: A shy child can wave, offer a seat, share a snack or show the water cooler and library, as Sarika did.

qa.q: How might Irawati have felt during the first lunch?
qa.a: Irawati was probably nervous and relieved to be invited, since she nodded, took an orange piece and smiled on the way back.

grounding: A child welcomes a new classmate with a wave, a seat, a snack and a tour, and even a shy child can do it.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: Teacher's note, Class 4. A new boy, Noor, joined today. Hafsa was sitting nearest the door. Before I could say anything, she stood up, said “Welcome, I'm Hafsa,” and pulled out the chair beside her. She showed him the shelf where the pencil box goes and gave him one of her biscuits at break. Noor did not say much, but he stayed close to her all day and copied her folding of the worksheet. Hafsa is usually quiet in class, so I was struck by how easily she took the lead. I will ask her to help him again tomorrow. Mr. Iqbal.

qa.q: Where did Hafsa show Noor the pencil box goes?
qa.a: On the shelf.

qa.q: How did the teacher feel about Hafsa's welcome?
qa.a: He was surprised and pleased, struck that Hafsa, who is usually quiet, took the lead so easily.

qa.q: How could Mr. Iqbal support this welcome further?
qa.a: He could ask Hafsa to help Noor again tomorrow, as he plans, and also let Noor meet other children.

qa.q: How might Noor have felt during the first day?
qa.a: Noor said little but stayed close to Hafsa all day, which suggests feeling unsure and comforted by her company.

grounding: A child says hello, offers a seat, shares a snack and shows the new student around, and the teacher observes.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: Monday. Ujjwal's diary. A new girl came today: Salma, from Hyderabad. Ma'am put her next to me. I wanted to say hello, but my mouth wouldn't work. I get like that with new people. So I smiled and pushed my extra pencil towards her, the good one with the eraser. She smiled back. At lunch she sat alone, and I couldn't make myself walk over. So I waved from my table and pointed at the empty chair next to me. She came! We didn't talk much. She showed me her tiffin, and I showed her mine. Tomorrow I'm going to try saying one full sentence.

qa.q: Where did Salma come from?
qa.a: Salma came from Hyderabad.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling when the words wouldn't come?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt shy and a little frustrated, wanting to welcome Salma but finding it hard to talk to new people.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal welcome Salma without many words?
qa.a: Ujjwal smiled, shared the good pencil and waved Salma over to the empty chair at lunch.

qa.q: What might Salma have felt when Ujjwal pointed to the chair?
qa.a: Salma probably felt relieved and welcomed, no longer eating alone on her first day.

grounding: Shows a shy child welcoming a new classmate with a smile, a shared pencil and a wave to an empty seat.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: When the new boy, Nitin, climbed off the tractor-trolley at the village school gate, clutching a city schoolbag, Uday was the first to walk up. “Namaste. I'm Uday. You're in our class.” Nitin nodded, eyes darting. Uday showed him everything: where to leave his chappals outside the classroom, the handpump that squeaks, the neem tree where they eat, and which step is broken. At lunch he tipped half his roasted chana into Nitin's hand. “My Aai makes it spicy. Tell me if it's too much.” Nitin ate a handful, coughed, laughed and asked for more.

qa.q: What did Uday tip into Nitin's hand?
qa.a: Uday tipped half his roasted chana into Nitin's hand.

qa.q: What was Nitin likely feeling when he arrived with darting eyes?
qa.a: Nitin was likely nervous and unsure in a new place, far from the city school he knew.

qa.q: Which of Uday's actions made Nitin feel included?
qa.a: Greeting him first, showing him practical things like the chappals and the broken step, and sharing his chana at lunch.

qa.q: What would change if nobody had walked up to Nitin at the gate?
qa.a: Nitin might have spent his first day alone and confused, not knowing the rules or where to eat.

grounding: Shows a child welcoming a new classmate with a hello, a tour and a shared snack, teaching inclusion.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage: When Zeynep arrived in Rosa's class in Berlin, she spoke almost no German. She stood by the door holding her new timetable upside down. Rosa jumped up. “Hallo! I'm Rosa!” Zeynep looked blank. Rosa pointed to herself: “Rosa.” Then to Zeynep, eyebrows raised. “Zeynep,” she whispered. Rosa grinned, turned the timetable the right way up and pointed to the empty seat beside her. At break, Rosa offered half her apple and showed her the toilets, the water fountain and the good swing. By the afternoon, Zeynep had taught her merhaba, and Rosa said it every time they passed in the corridor.

qa.q: What was Zeynep holding upside down?
qa.a: Zeynep was holding her new timetable upside down.

qa.q: What was Zeynep likely feeling at the door?
qa.a: Zeynep was likely nervous and lost, speaking almost no German in a new school.

qa.q: How did Rosa welcome Zeynep across the language gap?
qa.a: She used names and gestures, fixed the timetable, offered a seat and half her apple, and showed her the important places.

qa.q: What did learning merhaba show about the friendship?
qa.a: It showed the welcome went both ways, with Zeynep sharing her language and Rosa using it warmly.

grounding: Shows a child welcoming a new student who speaks another language with a seat, a snack and a tour.

subtype: Welcoming a guest or new classmate [Expressing]
passage:
The new boy, Abhinav, stood in the classroom doorway with a steel water bottle clutched to his chest while thirty faces stared at him.

Payal's stomach flipped for him. She hated talking to new people; her words always came out in a squeak. But the seat next to her was empty. She caught his eye, gave a small smile and patted the bench twice.

Abhinav came and sat down, stiff as a stick. At break Payal still couldn't think of anything clever to say, so she broke her sesame chikki in half and held out the bigger piece. He took it. "Thanks. Where's the… water tap?"

Payal pointed, then got up. "I'll show you." It came out only a little squeaky.

qa.q: What did Payal share with Abhinav at break?
qa.a: Her sesame chikki, broken in half, and she gave him the bigger piece.

qa.q: What was Payal feeling as she caught Abhinav's eye?
qa.a: Shy and nervous herself, but sympathetic; her stomach flipped for him because she knew how it feels to be stared at.

qa.q: How can a shy child welcome a newcomer, as Payal did?
qa.a: With small acts: a smile, patting the empty seat, sharing a snack and showing the way, without needing clever words.

qa.q: What might Abhinav have been feeling in the doorway?
qa.a: Anxious and exposed with thirty faces staring, clutching his bottle; the patted seat probably came as a relief.

grounding: It shows a shy child welcoming a new classmate with a smile, a seat, a shared snack and a guided walk.
